title: At the Straits: Singapore, 1819
description: You are a junior interpreter with Raffles' expedition. The British want a port near the Straits, but Singapore belongs to Johor and the throne is disputed. You must listen, inspect papers, and advise during two tense meetings.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the Straits.

player.name: junior-interpreter
player.role: Junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition
player.brief: You translate short exchanges, carry notes, and report what each side claims.

sharedContext.text: Raffles came to find a safe British base near the Straits. He quickly made a first agreement with the Temenggong, but that deal may not be legal because only the Sultan can grant land. A dispute over the Johor throne now shapes every choice.

spans.quote: British merchants trading with China complained that they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
the East India Company needed a station commanding the entrance to the China Sea.
only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company. And the Johor throne itself was disputed.

endings.title: Only a Local Deal
endings.summary: You advise stopping with the first agreement. The Company has permission from the Temenggong, but not from a Sultan. The legal weakness remains, and the post stands on shaky ground.

historicalOutcome.text: This does not match the record. Raffles moved beyond the first agreement, recognised Hussein, and signed a treaty on 6 February 1819.

spans.quote: The agreement had a weakness.

endings.divergence: The historical treaty never happens here, so the settlement lacks the broader legal claim Raffles sought.
reflectionQuestions: Why was the Temenggong's signature alone not enough?

endings.title: Treaty Signed at Singapore
endings.summary: You back the treaty. Hussein is recognised, the Company gains its trading post, and Farquhar is left to run the new settlement. Dutch objections begin at once, but the settlement survives.

historicalOutcome.text: This matches the record. A treaty was signed on 6 February 1819, Farquhar was appointed Resident and Commandant, and the Dutch protested immediately. The dispute was later settled in 1824.

spans.quote: On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
Raffles appointed Farquhar as Resident and Commandant and sailed for Bencoolen on 7 February

endings.divergence: This ending matches the historical outcome.

endings.title: A Cautious Delay
endings.summary: You urge delay. The talks do not collapse, but the moment passes. The British lose speed, and others may shape events before a firm treaty is made.

historicalOutcome.text: This differs from the record. In fact, Raffles recognised Hussein and signed a treaty within days of his arrival, then left Farquhar in charge.

endings.title: Challenge and Crisis
endings.summary: You argue against the deal. The meeting breaks into mistrust, and the British case becomes weaker just as Dutch objections loom. A port may still be possible later, but not through this united treaty.

historicalOutcome.text: This differs from the record. The treaty was signed, but Dutch protest still followed because they recognised Abdul Rahman and claimed Singapore lay in their sphere.

spans.quote: On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
They regarded Singapore as lying within their sphere and Sultan Abdul Rahman, whom they recognised, as the only lawful ruler of Johor.

endings.divergence: Here the alliance fails before signature instead of facing Dutch protest after signature.
